questions.subject: MATH
questions.learningObjective: Solve problems involving predicates and quantifiers.
questions.stem: Under this scenario, over a domain of 7 objects, altogether how many separate unary predicates (subsets of the domain) can be defined?

options.misconception: Wrong belief "excludes the empty predicate" gives 127, not 128.
Wrong belief "counts one predicate per element only" gives 14, not 128.
Wrong belief "uses ordered pairs instead of subsets" gives 49, not 128.

questions.explanation: A unary predicate corresponds exactly to the subset of domain elements satisfying it, and an 7-element set has 2 to the power 7 subsets, so there are 128 distinct predicates.
questions.hint: A predicate is the same thing as the subset where it holds.

stimulus.body: In this variation, on a collection with 3 members, how many different binary relations are there?

questions.stem: In this variation, on a collection with 3 members, how many different binary relations are there?

options.misconception: Wrong belief "counts subsets rather than subsets of the Cartesian product" gives 8, not 512.
Wrong belief "counts ordered pairs but not choices of which pairs to include" gives 9, not 512.
Wrong belief "doubles the exponent instead of squaring it" gives 64, not 512.

questions.explanation: A binary relation is any subset of the Cartesian product, which has 3 times 3 equals 9 ordered pairs; choosing a subset of those pairs gives 2 to the power 9, namely 512.
questions.hint: A relation is a subset of the Cartesian product.

stimulus.body: For the sample case, on a collection with 3 members, how many different binary relations are there?

questions.stem: For the sample case, on a collection with 3 members, how many different binary relations are there?

options.misconception: Wrong belief "counts subsets rather than subsets of the Cartesian product" gives 8, not 512.
Wrong belief "counts ordered pairs but not choices of which pairs to include" gives 9, not 512.
Wrong belief "doubles the exponent instead of squaring it" gives 64, not 512.

questions.explanation: A binary relation is any subset of the Cartesian product, which has 3 times 3 equals 9 ordered pairs; choosing a subset of those pairs gives 2 to the power 9, namely 512.
questions.hint: A relation is a subset of the Cartesian product.

questions.stem: A problem asks: over a domain of 8 members, altogether how many different unary predicates (subsets of the domain) can be defined?

options.misconception: Wrong belief "excludes the empty predicate" gives 255, not 256.
Wrong belief "counts one predicate per element only" gives 16, not 256.
Wrong belief "uses ordered pairs instead of subsets" gives 64, not 256.

questions.explanation: A unary predicate corresponds exactly to the subset of domain elements satisfying it, and an 8-element set has 2 to the power 8 subsets, so there are 256 distinct predicates.
questions.hint: A predicate is the same thing as the subset where it holds.

questions.hint: Count arrangements of all the distinct hypotheses.

questions.subject: MATH
questions.learningObjective: Solve problems involving proof techniques and induction.
questions.stem: A proof by cases splits 9 possibilities into groups of size 6. How many groups are needed if the groups partition the possibilities?
questions.explanation: Partitioning 9 possibilities into groups of at most 6 requires the ceiling of 9 divided by 6, which is 2, because any leftover possibilities still need their own group. The required result is 2.
questions.hint: Round up because a partial group still counts.

options.misconception: Wrong belief "rounds down and loses the leftover case" gives 2, not 3.
Wrong belief "subtracts instead of dividing" gives 5, not 3.
Wrong belief "multiplies instead of dividing" gives 24, not 3.

questions.explanation: Partitioning 8 possibilities into groups of at most 3 requires the ceiling of 8 divided by 3, which is 3, because any leftover possibilities still need their own group.
questions.hint: Round up because a partial group still counts.

questions.stem: In the given setup, in in total how many different orders can 5 hypotheses be arranged in a linear proof chain?
questions.explanation: Ordering 5 distinct hypotheses in a line is a permutation, giving 5 factorial which equals 120. The required result is 120.
questions.hint: Count arrangements of all the distinct hypotheses.
